source.title: From Linear to Nonlinear: Provable Weak-to-Strong Generalization through Feature Learning
source.authors: Junsoo Oh; J.E. Song; Chulhee Yun

record.file_problem: The full paper, appendices, and checklist are present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: It analyzes and experimentally tests training a stronger model on a weaker model’s labels, but uses a theoretical feature-learning setup and test-error/accuracy comparisons rather than Burns et al.’s PGR measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper tests weak-to-strong training in a synthetic patch-data setting and on modified MNIST. Figure 1 gives qualitative accuracy results without extractable numerical values; these are recorded as figure-only. Cited findings from Burns et al. and other studies are not recorded as rows. The paper does not test auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling, or loss variants.
record.test_reason: The paper trains a weak linear CNN on true labels, then trains a stronger ReLU CNN on its pseudo-labels. It proves when the student beats the weak model (theorems) and measures test accuracy against the weak model on synthetic patch data and modified MNIST. It reports accuracy, not PGR, and has no measured true-label strong ceiling.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. More precisely: in the data-scarce regime, generalization arises through benign overfitting above a sample threshold and fails through harmful overfitting below it, with a tight transition. In the data-abundant regime it arises early through label correction, and overtraining is observed, not proven, to degrade it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the core recipe of a true-label-trained weak supervisor followed by gradient-based training of a stronger student on pseudo-labels. It studies linear-CNN-to-two-layer-ReLU-CNN theory and synthetic and modified-MNIST experiments, rather than pretrained language models or PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with pseudo-labeled training-set size and, in the data-abundant regime, with training stage/early stopping.

fits_no_version.finding: With abundant pseudo-labels, the student first generalizes near-perfectly. Continued training to fit the pseudo-labels then degrades test accuracy to about the weak model's level, as the student memorizes flipped-label hard-only examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overtraining on weak labels erases weak-to-strong gains as the student comes to fit the supervisor's errors; early stopping is needed (failure mode: imitating weak errors).

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful overfitting: with too few pseudo-labels, the student memorizes noise and its accuracy stays near the weak model's.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-to-strong gains require a minimum amount of weakly labeled data relative to the hard signal's strength.

record.problems: The theoretical conclusions rely on a simplified structured distribution and specific architectures and assumptions. The synthetic figure reports accuracy trends without numerical values or uncertainty. MNIST results are based on five independent runs; the checklist says no statistical significance measures are reported. The paper does not establish the exact PGR or a direct empirical strong-model true-label ceiling.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant reported outcomes were omitted. Training-loss curves and training accuracy were not added as rows where they do not measure the claim’s test-performance outcome.

untested.parts: PGR itself is never computed, since there is no empirically trained true-label strong ceiling. Gains are reported only as accuracy above the weak model.
All of it: no auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling or loss variants. The authors list confidence loss as future work.
Supervisor/student size sweeps, chess, reward modelling, and representation-based predictors. Only pseudo-label sample size, training stage and an SNR threshold are studied.
Exploitation of what the supervisor cannot check, distribution shift, and shrinking gains under correlated weak/strong errors.
Real vision tasks beyond a modified binary-parity MNIST with small CNN/MLP models.

record.verdict_notes: This is mainly a theoretical paper with small illustrative experiments. There is no PGR and no measured strong ceiling. MNIST uses five runs and no significance tests; the synthetic results are figure-only. The weak-model rows were baselines and have been unlinked. R4–R7 are probabilistic bounds under asymptotic conditions, not measurements.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compute PGR or compare with a numerically measured strong model trained on true labels; the theoretical zero-error strong model is an existence result.
Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, and loss variants are not tested.
Tests data-volume regimes and synthetic versus modified-MNIST tasks, but not a supervisor/student size sweep, chess, reward modelling, or representation-based predictors.
Tests harmful overfitting and degradation with continued training; does not test distribution shift or whether gains shrink when weak and strong models make correlated errors.
Provides theoretical conditions in a specific patch-data, linear-CNN-to-ReLU-CNN setting, not general conditions for arbitrary students and supervisors.
Tests modified MNIST only; no other vision datasets or modalities.

relation.reason: Provides original guarantees and experiments comparing weakly supervised students with their weak supervisors.

tranche.reason: Tests whether weak-label-trained students outperform supervisors through nonlinear CNN feature learning, using theoretical error bounds and accuracy experiments rather than the original pretrained-model setup.

source_check.notes: Late-phase degradation is empirical, not proved. MNIST uncertainty is SD over five runs; the supplied suggested-status statement makes no specific claim about this study.

statements.correction: Data-scarce benign-overfitting gains: proved in Theorem 3.4. Data-abundant early-phase gains: proved in Theorem 3.6. Late-phase degradation: empirically observed in Section 5.1; rigorous proof left open in Section 3.2.
statements.problem: The sentence presents loss of gains after overtraining as proved. The paper explicitly leaves a rigorous proof of late-phase degradation open.

statements.correction: Table 1: modified MNIST parity; MLP supervisor; three-convolutional-layer CNN student; full-batch Adam for 300 epochs; mean and SD over five runs. Training-duration degradation is tested separately on synthetic patch data in Section 5.1.
statements.problem: The conditions conflate the synthetic patch-data experiment with the modified-MNIST experiment. Comparing gains with marginal SDs does not establish statistical significance.
